name: Afghanistan Women’s National Team
subtitle: Football in exile
story:
In August 2021, the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Women and girls lost the freedom to play organised football. Members of the Afghanistan women’s national team were among the footballers and other athletes evacuated to Australia. Former captain Khalida Popal helped players find a way to safety.

In 2022, players began training together again in Melbourne. Melbourne Victory supported their return to the pitch, and the team entered local competition in Victoria. Playing together helped them keep their team and their Afghan identity alive while they rebuilt their lives.

In 2025, Afghan Women United brought together Afghan footballers living outside the country. They played at a FIFA series in Morocco. In April 2026, FIFA changed its rules to allow Afghan women to represent their country in official international matches. This followed years of advocacy by players and their supporters.

2022 · Players trained together again in Melbourne with Melbourne Victory’s support.
2026 · FIFA changed its rules to make official international representation possible.

name: North Korea Women’s National Team
subtitle: Three Asian titles and a World Cup return
story:
North Korea’s senior women’s team competes internationally as DPR Korea. It won the AFC Women’s Asian Cup in 2001, 2003 and 2008. The team’s best FIFA Women’s World Cup finish came in 2007 in China. A 2–0 win over Nigeria helped it reach the quarter-finals.

In March 2026, DPR Korea faced Chinese Taipei in a World Cup qualifying play-off on Australia’s Gold Coast. Hong Song Ok scored three goals in a 4–0 win that secured a place at Brazil 2027. It will be the team’s first Women’s World Cup since Germany 2011.

artwork.back: STAR Development Centre special edition SE03. Holm Ladies Football Team, Holm in Orkney, 1947. Eleven known players from a surviving team photograph. A recollection of a match with Kirkwall Ladies survives.

name: Margaret Flett & Holm Ladies
subtitle: A girl from Orkney's forgotten football team
story:
In 1947, eleven women and girls from Holm in Orkney posed together for a photograph. They wore striking dark-and-light football shirts, some with skirts and others with shorts. Behind them stood old cars; in the front row, the woman in the middle held a ball marked “HOLM LADIES 1947”. The photograph gives us a rare glimpse of local women's football in the years after the Second World War.

Kneeling at the far left of the front row was Margaret Flett. She is believed to have been about fourteen years old. She is remembered as a very fast, agile player, although surviving match records do not allow us to measure her performances or reconstruct her playing career. In the photograph she faces the camera in her quartered shirt and dark shorts: a young footballer who belonged to a team.

We know the names of the other players because people who recognised the photograph helped identify them. The back row is recorded as Elaine Crowther, Sally Peterson, Elma Kirkness, Lil Anderson, Janet Mair and Violet Flett. Alongside Margaret in the front row were Margaret Buchan, Madge Garriock, Elsie Buchan and Vera Garriock. Their names are an important part of the team's surviving history. Despite sharing a surname, we cannot confirm whether Margaret and Violet Flett were related.

One contributor to the Orkney Image Library remembered Kirkwall Ladies visiting Holm and winning 10–0. This is a community recollection, not a verified contemporary match report. We do not yet know how many matches Holm played, how long the team lasted, or what Margaret did later in life.

The mystery is part of why this card matters. Football history is not only about famous internationals and trophies. It also belongs to the girls who pulled on a shirt and played for their local community, even when few people wrote down their achievements. Margaret and her teammates deserve to be remembered.
facts: 1947 · A surviving photograph records the Holm Ladies Football Team in Orkney.
Margaret Flett · Identified at the far left of the front row; believed to be about fourteen.
11 players · Their names were identified through local archive contributions.
Kirkwall match · A 10–0 score survives as an unverified community recollection.

name: Robbins Gloving Factory Ladies
subtitle: From the glove factory to the football pitch
story:
Look closely at the surviving team photograph and you can see a small robin on the players’ shirts. Some hold trophies and one holds a football. Somerset Council lists the photograph under 1936, while the Community Heritage Access Centre dates it to around the mid-1930s.

Several of the women worked at Edwin ‘Tink’ Robbins’ glove factory on Alexandra Road in Yeovil. The South Somerset Heritage Collection records that Edwin organised games and that the team won a cup. The Community Heritage Access Centre identifies him in the back row of the photograph.

The club’s bird is the detail that makes this team instantly recognisable. It links the women’s football shirts to the name of the factory where they worked. The surviving sources used here leave the name of the cup and the final score open.

name: Bath Ladies AFC
subtitle: From Bath to a packed Old Trafford
story:
In 1921, Bath Ladies AFC played Dick, Kerr Ladies of Preston at Old Trafford. The National Football Museum estimates that between 25,000 and 30,000 people watched. Between 1920 and 1921 Bath played at least ten games and raised more than £3,000 for post-war charities.

Dorothy Harrison served as captain and vice-captain at different times. Her sisters Edie, Mabel and Audley played alongside her. The team's distinctive hockey-style kit appears in surviving photographs, including pictures from their match against Plymouth.

In June 1922, the players and officials presented their honorary secretary and treasurer, Alfred Edward Manns, with a silver case. Its reverse carries 24 names. The engraving preserves the names of people who helped make the team possible.

artwork.back: Somerset Football Heritage. The Super Strikers. An illustrated indoor six-a-side court and a timeline from the Super Strikers in 1993 to Keynsham Town Ladies FC in 1998/99.

name: Keynsham Super Strikers
subtitle: The schoolgirls who started a club
story:
In 1993, a group of girls from Chandag Primary in Keynsham wanted a football team. According to the club’s history, their sports teacher was already busy with the boys’ team and dismissed the idea of girls playing. The girls took their idea to Barrie Newton and asked him to help them start a team. They called themselves the Super Strikers and entered a local under-11 league, playing six-a-side indoors.

For about three years, six-a-side was their regular game. More players joined, and eventually the club had enough players to arrange occasional eleven-a-side friendlies. That meant trying a different version of the same game. An indoor court puts teammates close together, while a full-size pitch gives players more space to cover and more choices about where to move when they don’t have the ball.

A local telecommunications company, Protel, sponsored the team during those early years. The club became Protel Super Strikers and adopted a Celtic-style green-and-white kit. The hoops on the front of this card are inspired by that later kit. The court on the back takes you back to the team’s first games.

In 1998/99, the club took the name Keynsham Town Ladies FC, linked up with Keynsham Town’s men’s club and shared its facilities. In their first season in Division Two of the South West Women’s League, they finished third. Just six years earlier, the founders had been schoolgirls asking for help to get a team going. Their first step was small enough to fit on an indoor court. It gave other girls a team to join and, over time, made eleven-a-side football possible.
facts: 1993 · Girls from Chandag Primary founded the Super Strikers.
Under-11 · They started in a local six-a-side league.
Protel · A local sponsor gave the team its second name.
1998/99 · Keynsham Town Ladies finished third in Division Two.

name: Beryl Pugh
subtitle: The referee who qualified
story:
In 1957, schoolteacher Beryl Pugh passed a refereeing test administered by the Somerset FA. She had already taken charge of a school football match when she stood in for the sports master. Some people laughed at seeing a woman referee. Beryl later explained that their reaction made her more determined to qualify and demonstrate that women belonged in football.

She took the examination and passed. Yet the recognition she received was different from that given to male referees. According to the National Football Museum, Somerset FA supplied written confirmation of her success, but did not give her the certificate that men received.

Her story asks us to look beyond the result of an examination. Passing a test shows that a person has met its requirements. Being treated differently afterwards raises another question. What happens when someone proves their knowledge, but the organisation recognising it still treats them unequally?

For a referee, preparation matters. Knowing the Laws of the Game helps an official explain decisions, recognise offences and restart play correctly. Players also have a part to play. Listening to an explanation and speaking respectfully can help everyone understand what has happened, even when a decision is disappointing.

Beryl’s experience offers a starting point for thinking about that respect. Imagine arriving at a school game, ready to do a job, and being laughed at before making a decision. What would help you feel welcome? A captain’s greeting, teammates who listen, or an adult who challenges the laughter could all make a difference. This card remembers Beryl’s achievement and invites you to consider how you welcome the next person who steps onto your pitch.

name: Yeovil Town Ladies
subtitle: Somerset’s 2016 champions

artwork.front: STAR Somerset Football Heritage special edition SE08. Yeovil Town Ladies, FA WSL 2 champions 2016. An illustrated celebration of women in green-and-white hoops embracing at a football ground, framed in emerald and gold. Imagined players commemorate the team.
artwork.back: Yeovil Town Ladies. Champions 2016. 6 November, Huish Park. Yeovil Town 3–0 Sheffield. Lucy Quinn opened the scoring, Annie Heatherson headed in the second and Nicola Cousins completed the win. FA WSL 2 title won on goal difference. Illustrated celebration with a football, green-and-white scarf, supporters and floodlights.

story:
By the end of October 2016, Yeovil Town Ladies had secured something special. A 2–0 victory away to London Bees guaranteed promotion to FA WSL 1, the top division. Kayleigh Green and Nadia Lawrence scored the goals for Jamie Sherwood’s side. Promotion was settled, but the title still had to be won.

On 6 November, Yeovil welcomed Sheffield to Huish Park for the final league match. Bristol City were also chasing first place. Lucy Quinn gave Yeovil an early advantage, firing in the opening goal after 15 minutes. At half-time, news that Bristol were four goals ahead against Oxford added pressure. Yeovil needed to finish their own job.

Annie Heatherson responded almost immediately after the restart, heading in a cross from Kayleigh Green. Later, Nicola Cousins sent a ball in from the right that found the bottom corner. The final score was 3–0. Yeovil were FA WSL 2 champions, finishing ahead of Bristol City on goal difference.

Captain Ellie Curson thanked the supporters and spoke about the pressure the team had discussed at half-time. Her reaction connected the achievement to everyone involved, including players, management and fans. A local Somerset team had earned its place in the top division and completed the season with a league title.

Think about the two stages of that finish. Yeovil first achieved promotion, then returned to compete for the championship. For your own football, you might celebrate reaching one goal and still choose something else to work towards. During a difficult match, focusing on your next pass, movement or challenge can give you a manageable task. Which action helps you concentrate when the score matters?

name: Las Pioneras
subtitle: Argentina’s pioneers at the Azteca

artwork.front: STAR Football Heritage SE09. Las Pioneras, Argentina 1971. A 1970s sky-blue, cream and gold illustrated poster, showing Argentina players celebrating before the Estadio Azteca. The stadium follows a 1970 archival panorama. Argentina 4–1 England, 21 August 1971. Elba Selva scored four goals. Unofficial world tournament. Illustrated reconstruction with imagined players.
artwork.back: Las Pioneras, Argentina, Mexico 1971. A period-inspired illustration of the Azteca, the 4–1 score and three facts about Elba Selva, the independent tournament and Women’s Footballer Day. Old boots, a football and a commemorative ticket complete the design.

story:
On 21 August 1971, Argentina’s women walked onto the pitch at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. Their opponents were England, and the occasion was an international women’s tournament held independently of FIFA. These players would later become known as Las Pioneras: the pioneers.

Elba Selva wore number 10. A left-footed player who had loved football since childhood, she had grown up facing the idea that the game belonged to boys. By 1971, she was a mother and a factory worker as well as a footballer. Travelling to Mexico meant making a difficult decision about work and family. Her husband encouraged her to take the opportunity.

The team’s resources were limited. They arrived without the kit and boots that a modern national squad would expect, receiving help in Mexico. Against England, Selva scored four times. Argentina won 4–1 in one of football’s most famous stadiums. Her goals gave the team a victory that would eventually become a landmark in the country’s sporting memory.

Argentina finished fourth in the tournament. Yet their achievement received little lasting attention at home. Decades later, former goalkeeper Lucila Sandoval helped bring the players together and share their stories. The date of the England match became Argentina’s Women’s Footballer Day.

Remembering this team means looking beyond a score. It means noticing the women who made room for themselves in a sport that offered them little support. Their story also shows why keeping photographs, names and memories matters.

For your own football, think of someone whose encouragement helps you play. What opportunity would you like to try, and what practical support would make that possible?

A lasting legacy · 21 August became Argentina’s Women’s Footballer Day.
